title: The Ice Pause Is Over | Rapid Arctic Melting Fractures Global Polar Bear Populations
description: Arctic sea ice hit record winter lows, devastating Western Hudson Bay polar bears while forcing Barents Sea populations to adapt to land food sources.

content_html:
TROMSOE, Norway — For a few brief years in the early 2020s, climate skeptics pointed to a temporary stabilization in winter Arctic sea ice loss as proof that the melting had slowed. Today, that pause is officially over, and the consequences for the Arctic's apex predator are becoming severe and geographically fractured.

A major study published in PNAS confirmed that recent exceptionally low winters shattered the brief stabilization period, locking the Arctic into a permanent, significant downward trend. On March 22, the Arctic sea ice reached its lowest maximum extent in the 47-year satellite record, dropping to a mere 14.33 million square kilometers. Regions like the Gulf of St. Lawrence remained almost entirely ice-free throughout the winter. OzoneNews's animals and wildlife beat has been tracking polar bear population data across multiple Arctic subpopulations as the ice retreats at an accelerating pace.

Even worse, the composition of the ice has fundamentally changed. The Arctic has lost nearly 47% of its thick, multi-year ice compared to the 1980s. The ice cap is now predominantly thin, seasonal ice that melts rapidly in the spring, leaving almost no old ice remaining. For the roughly 26,000 polar bears globally that rely entirely on this ice to hunt seals, this rapid melting has created starkly different realities depending on where they live.

The Hardest Hit | Western Hudson Bay

In Canada's Western Hudson Bay, the situation is increasingly desperate. The ice-free season in this region has extended by a full month, now lasting over five months compared to just four in the 1980s. Because polar bears require sea ice as a platform to hunt energy-dense ringed and bearded seals, this extra month forces them ashore far earlier. Trapped on land, they are completely cut off from their primary food source, forcing them to burn through critical fat reserves.

As a direct result of this prolonged starvation period, the Western Hudson Bay polar bear subpopulation has plummeted by approximately 50%. Mothers are struggling to produce enough milk for their cubs, jeopardizing the survival of the next generation. The Polar Bears International study quantifies the direct bioenergetic link between sea ice loss and population decline, confirming that the mechanism is starvation driven by lost hunting access.

The environment desk has reported on how the loss of multi-year ice is creating feedback loops that accelerate warming in the Arctic faster than any other region on Earth, a phenomenon known as Arctic amplification.

The Resilient Exception | The Barents Sea

In stark contrast, scientists tracking bears in the Barents Sea between Norway and Russia reported a surprising bit of qualified optimism. Even though the Barents Sea is warming faster than almost any other part of the Arctic, the body condition and reproduction rates of polar bears in this specific region have remained remarkably stable.

Biologists discovered that these specific bears are exhibiting extreme behavioral plasticity. To survive the ice loss, they are shifting their diets to land-based food sources they historically ignored, including hunting reindeer and scavenging on unusually abundant alternative marine mammal carcasses that wash ashore. Research published in Scientific Reports has documented how Svalbard's polar bears are maintaining body condition despite significant sea ice loss in their region.

However, the IUCN Polar Bear Specialist Group and leading researchers warn that this land-based scavenging is strictly a temporary buffer. A polar bear's physiology is evolved to process the massive, lipid-rich blubber of marine seals. Terrestrial foods like bird eggs, berries, or lean reindeer meat simply do not provide enough caloric density to support their massive body size long-term. If the ice caps continue their current trajectory, even the most adaptable populations like those in the Barents Sea will eventually cross a threshold where they can no longer find enough energy to survive. A documentary analysis of the bioenergetic modeling shows how researchers directly link climate-driven ice loss with the dramatic population decline in Western Hudson Bay.

The Arctic is not melting uniformly, and neither are its polar bear populations responding uniformly. But the underlying driver, the loss of the ice platform that sustains the entire Arctic marine food web, is accelerating everywhere. The question is not whether polar bears will adapt, but how many subpopulations will run out of time before they do.
